final_method_items.reason: Strongest fix location among the listed methods. The bug is specifically an incorrect 32-bit x86 move of an 8-byte object using DFmode/x87 machinery, and this function explicitly handles moves of `DI, DF, XF, and TF` values on i386. It sits exactly where an 8-byte union copy misclassified as DFmode would be split into concrete instructions, making it the most direct place to prevent `fldl`/`fstpl` from being used for representation-preserving copies.

final_method_items.summary: If STMT kills the memory reference REF return true, otherwise return false.
final_method_items.reason: Best match to the reported failure mechanism. The bug hinges on GCC not recognizing that `MCOp.IntVal = Val` fully overwrites the union storage and should kill any earlier `DoubleVal`-based interpretation before `dest = MCOp` is optimized. This function is the main alias-oracle entry that decides whether a statement completely kills a prior memory reference, exactly the kind of stale liveness/type-tracking mistake described in the report.

final_method_items.summary: If there's a chance to get a pseudo for t then if it would be of float mode and the actual access is via an integer mode (lowered memcpy or similar access) then avoid the register expansion if the mode likely is not storage suitable for raw bits processing (like XFmode on i?86).
final_method_items.reason: Very plausible root-cause area. Its documented purpose is extremely close to the bug: avoid register expansion when storage has float mode but accesses are really raw integer/bitwise operations on i386-like targets. The reproducer is essentially stale floating storage being copied after an integer overwrite, so failure to apply this logic could let the union live in a float-shaped pseudo and later be copied through x87.

behavior_items: The program defines a union `MyClass` with two overlapping 64-bit views of the same storage: `int64_t IntVal` and `double DoubleVal`. Because both members occupy the same bytes, writing through one member determines the exact raw bit pattern later observed through the other member.

The default constructor `MyClass() : DoubleVal(0.0) {}` is important because it makes GCC treat the object as having been initialized through the floating-point member. That constructor writes the 64-bit IEEE-754 encoding of `0.0` into the union storage before any integer assignment happens.

Inside `create(MyClass &dest, int64_t Val)`, a local union object `MCOp` is first default-constructed, so its bytes become the `double` representation of zero. Immediately after that, `MCOp.IntVal = Val;` overwrites the same 8 bytes with the caller-provided integer bit pattern.

The value passed from `main` is `0xfff0000000000001`, which is not just an arbitrary 64-bit integer: interpreted as an IEEE-754 double bit pattern, it is a signaling NaN. As raw integer data, it should be copied bit-for-bit without any semantic change.

The statement `dest = MCOp;` performs a union copy. At the C++ source level this is meant to copy the object representation, preserving all 64 bits exactly, regardless of whether those bits also form a meaningful `double` value.

The reproducer depends on x86-32 code generation with optimization enabled (`-O3 -m32`, though the report says `-O1` through `-O3` all fail). On this target, GCC 4.6.3 sometimes chooses x87 floating-point load/store instructions (`fldl`/`fstpl`) to move 8-byte values when it believes the object is suitably associated with a `double`.

Using `fldl`/`fstpl` is incorrect for this copy because those instructions do not behave like a pure byte move when the bit pattern denotes a signaling NaN. Loading the 64-bit pattern as an x87 floating-point value canonicalizes it: the signaling NaN is quieted and the payload bits may be altered according to x87 NaN rules.

As a result, the store back with `fstpl` writes a different 64-bit pattern than the original integer bits. The union copy therefore becomes value-transforming instead of representation-preserving, violating the source program’s expected semantics for copying the union object.

The observable failure is that `create(copy, magic);` returns with `copy.IntVal` containing a quiet-NaN encoding rather than the original signaling-NaN encoding. `printf` shows different hexadecimal values for `magic` and `copy.IntVal`, and the `assert(magic == copy.IntVal);` fails.

The bug is highly sensitive to the constructor member chosen. If the constructor is changed to `MyClass() : IntVal(0) {}`, GCC no longer treats the temporary as needing floating-point-style transfer, so it uses ordinary integer/memory moves and the raw 64-bit pattern is copied correctly.

That contrast demonstrates the central issue: the compiler’s optimization is keyed off the fact that the union’s `double` member was used at some point, not whether a floating-point interpretation is still semantically relevant at the copy site. After `MCOp.IntVal = Val;`, the live meaning of the bytes for this operation is just opaque object representation.

The reproducer therefore exercises a miscompilation in alias/representation tracking or move selection: GCC propagates stale type information from the earlier `DoubleVal` initialization into the later copy, and that stale information causes it to choose a non-bit-preserving transfer mechanism.

The fact that GCC 4.8 reportedly succeeds indicates the bug was later fixed, likely by making the compiler avoid x87-based copying for such union/object moves unless it is safe to treat the bytes as an actual floating-point value, or by using a plain integer/block move instead.

The extra flags shown in the report (`-fno-strict-aliasing`, `-fwrapv`, warnings, `noinline`) mostly help stabilize the reproducer and rule out unrelated optimizations. `noinline` keeps `create` visible as a separate function so the problematic temporary construction and copy sequence remains easy for the compiler to lower in the failing way.

Semantically, the test is not about arithmetic on NaNs; it is about exact preservation of object bits during copy. The signaling-NaN constant is chosen precisely because it exposes the difference between a true memory copy and a floating-point load/store round-trip, which would otherwise appear harmless for ordinary bit patterns.
test_behavior_analysis.summary: This reproducer creates a union whose storage is first initialized through its `double` member, then overwritten through its `int64_t` member with a bit pattern that represents an IEEE-754 signaling NaN, and finally copied to another union object. Correct behavior requires a raw 64-bit copy of the object representation. GCC 4.6.3 on x86-32 miscompiles the copy by using x87 `fldl`/`fstpl` as if the bytes were still meaningfully a `double`; that floating-point round-trip quiets the signaling NaN and changes the stored bits. The failure only appears when the earlier constructor touched `DoubleVal`, showing that GCC incorrectly lets a dead floating-point interpretation influence later union-copy code generation.

test_failure_analysis.analysis: The common pattern is a miscompile of a union/object-representation copy on x86-32 where GCC preserves stale floating-point type information from an earlier write to the union's `double` member, even though a later write through the `int64_t` member fully overwrites the storage before the copy. The failure only appears under optimization and only when the constructor initializes `DoubleVal`, which strongly indicates a middle-end or i386 backend optimization that classifies the 8-byte union copy as a floating-point move instead of a raw bitwise move. Because the copied bits are an sNaN encoding, using x87 `fldl`/`fstpl` changes the payload into a qNaN, so the generated code violates C++ object-copy semantics by performing a value-transforming FP load/store instead of preserving the exact 64-bit representation. The fact that initializing through `IntVal` avoids the bug, and that newer GCC versions no longer fail, points to a defect in liveness/type-tracking for union contents or in the x86 move-selection logic for 64-bit copies involving union/BLKmode objects.
possible_causes: Incorrect union liveness/type tracking in the middle end: after `MCOp.IntVal = Val`, GCC still marks the union as effectively `double`-typed because of the constructor store to `DoubleVal`, causing later copy expansion to use floating-point moves for dead/stale type information.

Bug in copy/move expansion for small aggregates or unions on i386: the compiler selects x87 `fldl`/`fstpl` for an 8-byte union assignment based on member type history rather than requiring a guaranteed bit-preserving move such as integer registers or `memcpy`-style block copy.

Defect in alias/object-representation handling for unions: GCC treats a union copy as a typed copy of the last known floating-point view instead of an opaque copy of bytes, violating semantics when the active bits were last written through a different member.

i386 backend predicate/cost model bug for 64-bit transfers: the backend considers x87 register moves valid for copying DFmode-like data even when the source object is semantically just raw storage and may contain noncanonical NaN bit patterns that must not be normalized.

Failure in dead-store or dataflow analysis around constructor initialization: the earlier `DoubleVal(0.0)` store should become irrelevant after the full-width `IntVal` overwrite, but GCC appears to let that dead initialization influence mode selection at the later `dest = MCOp` copy site.

Mode mismatch during RTL expansion or combine/reload: an 8-byte union/object move may be lowered as `DFmode` because the object once flowed through a floating member, instead of staying in `DImode` or `BLKmode`, leading to backend emission of `fldl`/`fstpl` and bit corruption for sNaN patterns.
evidence: The failure requires this exact sequence: initialize union through `DoubleVal`, overwrite through `IntVal`, then copy the union; removing the `DoubleVal` constructor use makes the program work.
The observed wrong-code mechanism is explicit: GCC 4.6.3 on x86-32 emits x87 `fldl`/`fstpl` for the 64-bit copy, and these instructions canonicalize signaling NaNs instead of preserving raw bits.
The copied constant `0xfff0000000000001` is chosen because as a double bit pattern it is an sNaN, so any accidental floating-point interpretation immediately exposes a non-bitwise copy.
At source level, `dest = MCOp;` is a union/object copy and must preserve the object representation exactly; the assertion failure shows GCC transformed the bits during code generation.
The bug reproduces across `-O1` to `-O3` on `-m32`, suggesting an optimization/codegen path common to optimized i386 builds rather than undefined behavior in the test.
Using `MyClass() : IntVal(0) {}` instead of `DoubleVal(0.0)` avoids x87 moves and the copy is correct, tying the defect specifically to stale floating-member influence on move selection.
The report notes GCC 4.8 succeeds while 4.6 and 4.7 fail, consistent with a compiler bug later fixed in union-copy/type-mode handling rather than a problem in the reproducer.

selected_files.reason: Most suspicious because the bug is x86-32 specific and manifests as choosing x87 `fldl`/`fstpl` for an 8-byte union copy. This file contains core i386 target hooks, move-cost logic, mode handling, and backend decisions that commonly determine whether a DFmode-style floating move is used instead of a raw integer/BLK move.

Highly likely because the observed bad code is emitted as x87 load/store instructions, and the machine description controls move patterns and alternatives for DFmode/DImode/BLKmode on i386. A wrong or overpermissive move pattern here could allow union/object copies to be lowered as floating-point transfers.

Very plausible middle-end source of the bug because union assignment should be expanded as an object-representation copy. If small aggregate/union copy expansion here reuses stale mode information and treats the 8-byte object as DFmode rather than opaque storage, it would directly trigger x87-based copying.

Likely involved because this is where GIMPLE/trees are lowered into RTL and object copies receive machine modes during expansion. The reported stale influence from the earlier `DoubleVal` initialization suggests a mode-selection or expansion bug at this tree-to-RTL boundary.

Strong candidate since it contains i386-specific expansion helpers for multiword and double-mode operations. If an 8-byte union copy is being split or expanded according to floating-point mode history rather than true object-copy semantics, the bug could originate here.

Possible because move/copy expansion for scalar modes often flows through optabs, including target-selected move strategies. An incorrect decision to materialize an 8-byte copy as a DFmode move instead of an integer move could arise from generic move-expansion logic here.

Moderately suspicious because the report strongly suggests stale type/representation information survives after a full-width overwrite of the union through `IntVal`. If alias/object representation tracking fails to model that overwrite precisely, later expansion could still believe the object is meaningfully `double`-typed.

Possible contributor because SRA and aggregate scalarization interact directly with unions and field-based accesses. A mistaken scalarized view that preserves the floating member identity past the integer overwrite could bias later copy lowering toward DFmode.

Less likely than expansion, but still plausible because combine can rewrite RTL moves into cheaper target-specific forms after initial lowering. If a safe integer/memory copy is combined into an x87 move sequence due to mode confusion, this pass could be responsible.

Relevant because the final bad instructions are x87 stack-register operations. While it probably does not create the semantic mistake, it is a plausible location if x87 stack conversion preserves or introduces the unsafe `fldl`/`fstpl` sequence for what should remain a bit-preserving copy.

For these modes, the generic vector support in gcc will choose some non-vector mode in order to implement the type. Assume the number of st registers that are zeroed is num_of_st, we will emit the following sequence to zero them together: fldz; \ fldz; \ ... fldz; \ fstp %%st(0); \ fstp %%st(0); \ ... fstp %%st(0); i.e., num_of_st fldz followed by num_of_st fstp to clear the stack mark stack slots empty. How to compute the num_of_st: There is no direct mapping from stack registers to hard register numbers. If one stack register needs to be cleared, we don't know where in the stack the value remains. So, if any stack register needs to be cleared, the whole stack should be cleared. However, x87 stack registers that hold the return value should be excluded. x87 returns in the top (two for complex values) register, so num_of_st should be 7/6 when x87 returns, otherwise it will be 8. return the value of num_of_st.

LEN_TYPE is the type of the expression that was used to calculate it, and CTZ_LEN is the known trailing-zeros count of LEN, so LEN must be a multiple of 1<<CTZ_LEN even if it's not constant. The set of allowed stack pointer modifications is small: (1) One or more auto-inc style memory references (aka pushes), (2) One or more addition/subtraction with the SP as destination, (3) A single move insn with the SP as destination, (4) A call_pop insn, (5) Noreturn call insns if !ACCUMULATE_OUTGOING_ARGS. Insns in the sequence that do not modify the SP are ignored, except for noreturn calls. The return value is the amount of adjustment that can be trivially verified, via immediate operand or auto-inc. If the adjustment cannot be trivially extracted, the return value is HOST_WIDE_INT_MIN.

May return false if asked to push a partial argument during a sibcall optimization (as specified by SIBCALL_P) and the incoming and outgoing pointers cannot be shown to not overlap. ALIGN (in bits) is maximum alignment we can assume. If PARTIAL and REG are both nonzero, then copy that many of the first bytes of X into registers starting with REG, and push the rest of X. The amount of space pushed is decreased by PARTIAL bytes. REG must be a hard register in this case. If REG is zero but PARTIAL is not, take any all others actions for an argument partially in registers, but do not actually load any registers. EXTRA is the amount in bytes of extra space to leave next to this arg. This is ignored if an argument block has already been allocated. On a machine that lacks real push insns, ARGS_ADDR is the address of the bottom of the argument block for this call. We use indexing off there to store the arg. On mac

This provides a recursive shortcut back to store_constructor when it isn't necessary to go through store_field. gcc/expr.cc.signature: void store_constructor (tree exp, rtx target, int cleared, poly_int64 size, bool reverse)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Store the value of constructor EXP into the rtx TARGET. TARGET is either a REG or a MEM; we know it cannot conflict, since safe_from_p has been called. CLEARED is true if TARGET is known to have been zero'd. SIZE is the number of bytes of TARGET we are allowed to modify: this may not be the same as the size of EXP if we are assigning to a field which has been packed to exclude padding bits. If REVERSE is true, the store is to be done in reverse order.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: static rtx store_field (rtx target, poly_int64 bitsize, poly_int64 bitpos, poly_uint64 bitregion_start, poly_uint64 bitregion_end, machine_mode mode, tree exp, alias_set_type alias_set, bool nontemporal, bool reverse)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Store the value of EXP (an expression tree) into a subfield of TARGET which has mode MODE and occupies BITSIZE bits, starting BITPOS bits from the start of TARGET. If MODE is VOIDmode, it means that we are storing into a bit-field. BITREGION_START is bitpos of the first bitfield in this region. BITREGION_END is the bitpos of the ending bitfield in this region. These two fields are 0, if the C++ memory model does not apply, or we are not interested in keeping track of bitfield regions. Always return const0_rtx unless we have something particular to return. ALIAS_SET is the alias set for the destination. This value will (in general) be different from that for TARGET, since TARGET is a reference to the containing structure. If NONTEMPORAL is true, try generating a nontemporal store. If REVERSE is true, the store is to be done in reverse order.

gcc/expr.cc.signature: tree get_inner_reference (tree exp, poly_int64 *pbitsize, poly_int64 *pbitpos, tree *poffset, machine_mode *pmode, int *punsignedp, int *preversep, int *pvolatilep)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Given an expression EXP that may be a COMPONENT_REF, a BIT_FIELD_REF, an ARRAY_REF, or an ARRAY_RANGE_REF, look for nested operations of these codes and find the ultimate containing object, which we return. We set *PBITSIZE to the size in bits that we want, *PBITPOS to the bit position, *PUNSIGNEDP to the signedness and *PREVERSEP to the storage order of the field. If the position of the field is variable, we store a tree giving the variable offset (in units) in *POFFSET. This offset is in addition to the bit position. If the position is not variable, we store 0 in *POFFSET. If any of the extraction expressions is volatile, we store 1 in *PVOLATILEP. Otherwise we don't change that. If the field is a non-BLKmode bit-field, *PMODE is set to VOIDmode. Otherwise, it is a mode that can be used to access the field. If the field describes a variable-sized object, *PMODE is set to BLKmode and *PBITSIZE is set to -1. An access cannot be made in this case, but the address of the object can be found.

(CONST_INT ...)) or a nest of (PLUS ...) and (MINUS ...) where the terms are products as above, or REG or MEM, or constant. gcc/expr.cc.summary: Optimize x % C1 == C2 for signed modulo if C1 is a power of two and C2 is non-zero and C3 ((1<<(prec-1)) | (C1 - 1)): for C2 > 0 to x & C3 == C2 for C2 < 0 to x & C3 == (C2 & C3).

gcc/expr.cc.signature: enum tree_code maybe_optimize_mod_cmp (enum tree_code code, tree *arg0, tree *arg1)
gcc/expr.cc.summary: Attempt to optimize unsigned (X % C1) == C2 (or (X % C1) != C2). If C1 is odd to: (X - C2) * C3 <= C4 (or >), where C3 is modular multiplicative inverse of C1 and 1<<prec and C4 is ((1<<prec) - 1) / C1 or ((1<<prec) - 1) / C1 - 1 (the latter if C2 > ((1<<prec) - 1) % C1). If C1 is even, S = ctz (C1) and C2 is 0, use ((X * C3) r>> S) <= C4, where C3 is modular multiplicative inverse of C1>>S and 1<<prec and C4 is (((1<<prec) - 1) / (C1>>S)) >> S. For signed (X % C1) == 0 if C1 is odd to (all operations in it unsigned): (X * C3) + C4 <= 2 * C4, where C3 is modular multiplicative inverse of (unsigned) C1 and 1<<prec and C4 is ((1<<(prec - 1) - 1) / C1). If C1 is even, S = ctz(C1), use ((X * C3) + C4) r>> S <= (C4 >> (S - 1)) where C3 is modular multiplicative inverse of (unsigned)(C1>>S) and 1<<prec and C4 is ((1<<(prec - 1) - 1) / (C1>>S)) & (-1<<S). See the Hacker's Delight book, section 10-17.

gcc/expr.cc.summary: Generate code to calculate OPS, and exploded expression using a store-flag instruction and return an rtx for the result. OPS reflects a comparison. If TARGET is nonzero, store the result there if convenient. Return zero if there is no suitable set-flag instruction available on this machine. Once expand_expr has been called on the arguments of the comparison, we are committed to doing the store flag, since it is not safe to re-evaluate the expression. We emit the store-flag insn by calling emit_store_flag, but only expand the arguments if we have a reason to believe that emit_store_flag will be successful. If we think that it will, but it isn't, we have to simulate the store-flag with a set/jump/set sequence.

Since we are only interested in the lower 2 words, partial result (3) and the upper words of (2a) and (2b) don't need to be calculated. gcc/optabs.cc.signature: static rtx expand_doubleword_mod (machine_mode mode, rtx op0, rtx op1, bool unsignedp)
gcc/optabs.cc.summary: Subroutine of expand_binop. Optimize unsigned double-word OP0 % OP1 for constant OP1. If for some bit in [BITS_PER_WORD / 2, BITS_PER_WORD] range (prefer higher bits) ((1w << bit) % OP1) == 1, then the modulo can be computed in word-mode as ((OP0 & (bit - 1)) + ((OP0 >> bit) & (bit - 1)) + (OP0 >> (2 * bit))) % OP1. Whether we need to sum 2, 3 or 4 values depends on the bit value, if 2, then carry from the addition needs to be added too, i.e. like: sum += __builtin_add_overflow (low, high, &sum) Optimize signed double-word OP0 % OP1 similarly, just apply some correction factor to the sum before doing unsigned remainder, in the form of sum += (((signed) OP0 >> (2 * BITS_PER_WORD - 1)) & const); then perform unsigned remainder = sum % OP1; and finally remainder += ((signed) OP0 >> (2 * BITS_PER_WORD - 1)) & (1 - OP1);

(If the clz instruction produces the usual value at 0, which is K, the result of this code sequence will be -1; expand_ffs, below, relies on this. It might be nice to have it be K instead, for consistency with the (very few) processors that provide a ctz with a defined value, but that would take one more instruction, and it would be less convenient for expand_ffs anyway.

On failure, return CODE_FOR_nothing and leave *PTEST unchanged. Note that the comparison described by *PTEST should not be taken literally after a successful return. *PTEST is just a convenient place to store the two operands of the bit-and-test. If X and Y have mode BLKmode, then SIZE specifies the size of both X and Y. MODE is the mode of the inputs (in case they are const_int). COMPARISON is the rtl operator to compare with (EQ, NE, GT, etc.). It will be potentially converted into an unsigned variant based on UNSIGNEDP to select a proper jump instruction. PROB is the probability of jumping to LABEL. If the comparison is against zero then VAL contains the expression from which the non-zero RTL is derived.

gcc/optabs.cc.summary: This function expands the atomic store operation: Atomically store VAL in MEM. MEMMODEL is the memory model variant to use. USE_RELEASE is true if __sync_lock_release can be used as a fall back. function returns const0_rtx if a pattern was emitted.

gcc/optabs.cc.summary: See if there is a more optimal way to implement the operation "*MEM CODE VAL" using memory order MODEL. If AFTER is true the operation needs to return the value of *MEM after the operation, otherwise the previous value. TARGET is an optional place to place the result. The result is unused if it is const0_rtx. Return the result if there is a better sequence, otherwise NULL_RTX.

gcc/optabs.cc.signature: static rtx maybe_emit_op (const struct atomic_op_functions *optab, rtx target, rtx mem, rtx val, bool use_memmodel, enum memmodel model, bool after)
gcc/optabs.cc.summary: Try to emit an instruction for a specific operation varaition. OPTAB contains the OP functions. TARGET is an optional place to return the result. const0_rtx means unused. MEM is the memory location to operate on. VAL is the value to use in the operation. USE_MEMMODEL is TRUE if the variation with a memory model should be tried. MODEL is the memory model, if used. AFTER is true if the returned result is the value after the operation.

gcc/optabs.cc.signature: static rtx expand_atomic_fetch_op_no_fallback (rtx target, rtx mem, rtx val, enum rtx_code code, enum memmodel model, bool after)
gcc/optabs.cc.summary: This function expands an atomic fetch_OP or OP_fetch operation: TARGET is an option place to stick the return value. const0_rtx indicates the result is unused. atomically fetch MEM, perform the operation with VAL and return it to MEM. CODE is the operation being performed (OP) MEMMODEL is the memory model variant to use. AFTER is true to return the result of the operation (OP_fetch). AFTER is false to return the value before the operation (fetch_OP). This function will *only* generate instructions if there is a direct optab. No compare and swap loops or libcalls will be generated.

gcc/optabs.cc.signature: rtx expand_atomic_fetch_op (rtx target, rtx mem, rtx val, enum rtx_code code, enum memmodel model, bool after)

We do not assume that the containers of FIELD1 and FIELD2 are of the same type or size. Return 0 in case the base address of component_refs are same then FIELD1 and FIELD2 have same address. Note that FIELD1 and FIELD2 may not be of same type or size. Return 1 if FIELD1 and FIELD2 are non-overlapping. Return -1 otherwise. Main difference between 0 and -1 is to let nonoverlapping_component_refs_since_match_p discover the semantically equivalent part of the access path. gcc/tree-ssa-alias.cc.signature: static int nonoverlapping_refs_since_match_p (tree match1, tree ref1, tree match2, tree ref2, bool partial_overlap)
gcc/tree-ssa-alias.cc.summary: Try to disambiguate REF1 and REF2 under the assumption that MATCH1 and MATCH2 either point to the same address or are disjoint. MATCH1 and MATCH2 are assumed to be ref in the access path of REF1 and REF2 respectively or NULL in the case we established equivalence of bases. If PARTIAL_OVERLAP is true assume that the toplevel arrays may actually overlap by exact multiply of their element size. This test works by matching the initial segment of the access path and does not rely on TBAA thus is safe for !flag_strict_aliasing if match was determined without use of TBAA oracle. Return 1 if we can determine that component references REF1 and REF2, that are within a common DECL, cannot overlap. Return 0 if paths are same and thus there is nothing to disambiguate more (i.e. there is must alias assuming there is must alias between MATCH1 and MATCH2) Return -1 if we can not determine 0 or 1 - this happens when we met non-matching types was met in the path. In this case it may make sense to continue by other disambiguation oracles.

STMT_GSI is used to place newly created statements before the processed statement, REFRESH_GSI is used to place them afterwards - unless the processed statement must end a BB in which case it is placed on the outgoing non-EH edge. REFRESH_GSI and is then used to continue iteration over the BB. If sra_modify_expr is called only once with WRITE equal to true on a given statement, both iterator parameters can point to the same one.

For a call to .DEFERRED_INIT: var = .DEFERRED_INIT (size_of_var, init_type, name_of_var); examine the LHS variable VAR and replace it with a scalar replacement if there is one, also replace the RHS call to a call to .DEFERRED_INIT of the corresponding scalar relacement variable. Examine the subtree and do the scalar replacements in the subtree too. STMT is the call, GSI is the statment iterator to place newly created statement.

Examine both sides of the assignment statement pointed to by STMT, replace them with a scalare replacement if there is one and generate copying of replacements if scalarized aggregates have been used in the assignment. Set any scalar replacements of values in the constant pool to the initial value of the constant. Thus, we output statements like 'SR.1 = *.LC0[0];' into the function's entry block.
Traverse the function body and all modifications as decided in analyze_all_variable_accesses. Return true iff the CFG has been changed.
Generate statements initializing scalar replacements of parts of function parameters.
The "main" function of intraprocedural SRA passes. Runs the analysis and if it reveals there are components of some aggregates to be scalarized, it runs the required transformations.
Perform early intraprocedural SRA.
Perform "late" intraprocedural SRA.
If type T cannot be totally scalarized, return false. Otherwise return true and push to the vector within PC offsets and lengths of all padding in the type as total scalarization would encounter it.
Given two types in an assignment, return true either if any one cannot be totally scalarized or if they have padding (i.e. not copied bits)

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool can_combine_p (rtx_insn *insn, rtx_insn *i3, rtx_insn *pred ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED, rtx_insn *pred2 ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED, rtx_insn *succ, rtx_insn *succ2, rtx *pdest, rtx *psrc)

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool combinable_i3pat (rtx_insn *i3, rtx *loc, rtx i2dest, rtx i1dest, rtx i0dest, bool i1_not_in_src, bool i0_not_in_src, rtx *pi3dest_killed)

Consider: (set (reg:DI 101) (reg:DI 100)) (set (subreg:SI (reg:DI 101) 0) <foo>) This is NOT equivalent to: (parallel [(set (subreg:SI (reg:DI 100) 0) <foo>) (set (reg:DI 101) (reg:DI 100))]) Not only does this modify 100 (in which case it might still be valid if 100 were dead in I2), it sets 101 to the ORIGINAL value of 100. We can also run into a problem if I2 sets a register that I1 uses and I1 gets directly substituted into I3 (not via I2). In that case, we would be getting the wrong value of I2DEST into I3, so we must reject the combination. This case occurs when I2 and I1 both feed into I3, rather than when I1 feeds into I2, which feeds into I3. gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx subst (rtx x, rtx from, rtx to, bool in_dest, bool in_cond, bool unique_copy)

If they were modified, a record was made in undobuf so that undo_all will (among other things) return X to its original state. If the number of changes necessary is too much to record to undo, the excess changes are not made, so the result is invalid. The changes already made can still be undone. undobuf.num_undo is incremented for such changes, so by testing that the caller can tell whether the result is valid. `n_occurrences' is incremented each time FROM is replaced. IN_DEST is true if we are processing the SET_DEST of a SET. IN_COND is true if we are at the top level of a condition. UNIQUE_COPY is true if each substitution must be unique. We do this by copying if `n_occurrences' is nonzero.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx expand_compound_operation (rtx x)

ZERO_EXTEND is also considered "compound" because it can be replaced with an AND operation, which is simpler, though only one operation. The function expand_compound_operation is called with an rtx expression and will convert it to the appropriate shifts and AND operations, simplifying at each stage. The function make_compound_operation is called to convert an expression consisting of shifts and ANDs into the equivalent compound expression. It is the inverse of this function, loosely speaking.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static const_rtx expand_field_assignment (const_rtx x)

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx make_extraction (machine_mode mode, rtx inner, HOST_WIDE_INT pos, rtx pos_rtx, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT len, bool unsignedp, bool in_dest, bool in_compare)

If nonzero, a STRICT_LOW_PART will be used, if zero, ZERO_EXTEND or SIGN_EXTEND will be used. IN_COMPARE is true if we are in a COMPARE. This means that a ZERO_EXTRACT should be built even for bits starting at bit 0. MODE is the desired mode of the result (if IN_DEST == 0). This tells the caller to recurse on *X_PTR with IN_CODE equal to *NEXT_CODE_PTR, after which *X_PTR holds the final value. - Return a new rtx, which the caller returns directly.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: rtx make_compound_operation (rtx x, enum rtx_code in_code)

Return the new rtx, usually just X. Also, for machines like the VAX that don't have logical shift insns, try to convert logical to arithmetic shift operations in cases where they are equivalent. This undoes the canonicalizations to logical shifts done elsewhere. We try, as much as possible, to re-use rtl expressions to save memory. IN_CODE says what kind of expression we are processing. Normally, it is SET. In a memory address it is MEM. When processing the arguments of a comparison or a COMPARE against zero, it is COMPARE, or EQ if more precisely it is an equality comparison against zero.

Return a possibly simplified expression, but always convert X to MODE. If X is a CONST_INT, AND the CONST_INT with MASK. If JUST_SELECT is true, don't optimize by noticing that bits in MASK are all off in X. This is used when X will be complemented, by either NOT, NEG, or XOR.

gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X, a SET operation, can be rewritten as a bit-field assignment. Return that assignment if so. We only handle the most common cases.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx apply_distributive_law (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X is of the form (+ (* a c) (* b c)) and convert to (* (+ a b) c) if so.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx distribute_and_simplify_rtx (rtx x, int n)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: See if X is of the form (* (+ A B) C), and if so convert to (+ (* A C) (* B C)) and try to simplify. Most of the time, this results in no change. However, if some of the operands are the same or inverses of each other, simplifications will result. For example, (and (ior A B) (not B)) can occur as the result of expanding a bit field assignment. When we apply the distributive law to this, we get (ior (and (A (not B))) (and (B (not B)))), which then simplifies to (and (A (not B))). Note that no checks happen on the validity of applying the inverse distributive law. This is pointless since we can do it in the few places where this routine is called. N is the index of the term that is decomposed (the arithmetic operation, i.e. (+ A B) in the first example above). !N is the index of the term that is distributed, i.e. of C in the first example above.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_and_const_int_1 (scalar_int_mode mode, rtx varop, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT constop)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a logical `and' of VAROP with the constant CONSTOP, to be done in MODE. Return an equivalent form, if different from (and VAROP (const_int CONSTOP)). Otherwise, return NULL_RTX.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_and_const_int (rtx x, scalar_int_mode mode, rtx varop, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT constop)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: We have X, a logical `and' of VAROP with the constant CONSTOP, to be done in MODE. Return an equivalent form, if different from X. Otherwise, return X. If X is zero, we are to always construct the equivalent form.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx reg_nonzero_bits_for_combine (const_rtx x, scalar_int_mode xmode, scalar_int_mode mode, unsigned HOST_WIDE_INT *nonzero)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Given a REG X of mode XMODE, compute which bits in X can be nonzero. We don't care about bits outside of those defined in MODE. We DO care about all the bits in MODE, even if XMODE is smaller than MODE. For most X this is simply GET_MODE_MASK (GET_MODE (MODE)), but if X is a shift, AND, or zero_extract, we can do better.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx reg_num_sign_bit_copies_for_combine (const_rtx x, scalar_int_mode xmode, scalar_int_mode mode, unsigned int *result)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Given a reg X of mode XMODE, return the number of bits at the high-order end of X that are known to be equal to the sign bit. X will be used in mode MODE; the returned value will always be between 1 and the number of bits in MODE.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: unsigned int extended_count (const_rtx x, machine_mode mode, bool unsignedp)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return the number of "extended" bits there are in X, when interpreted as a quantity in MODE whose signedness is indicated by UNSIGNEDP. For unsigned quantities, this is the number of high-order zero bits. For signed quantities, this is the number of copies of the sign bit minus 1. In both case, this function returns the number of "spare" bits. For example, if two quantities for which this function returns at least 1 are added, the addition is known not to overflow. This function will always return 0 unless called during combine, which implies that it must be called from a define_split.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool merge_outer_ops (enum rtx_code *pop0, HOST_WIDE_INT *pconst0, enum rtx_code op1, HOST_WIDE_INT const1, machine_mode mode, bool *pcomp_p)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: This function is called from `simplify_shift_const' to merge two outer operations. Specifically, we have already found that we need to perform operation *POP0 with constant *PCONST0 at the outermost position. We would now like to also perform OP1 with constant CONST1 (with *POP0 being done last). Return true if we can do the operation and update *POP0 and *PCONST0 with the resulting operation. *PCOMP_P is set to true if we would need to complement the innermost operand, otherwise it is unchanged. MODE is the mode in which the operation will be done. No bits outside the width of this mode matter. It is assumed that the width of this mode is smaller than or equal to HOST_BITS_PER_WIDE_INT. If *POP0 or OP1 are UNKNOWN, it means no operation is required. Only NEG, PLUS, IOR, XOR, and AND are supported. We may set *POP0 to SET if the proper result is simply *PCONST0. If the resulting operation cannot be expressed as one operation, we return false and do not change *POP0, *PCONST0, and *PCOMP_P.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static scalar_int_mode try_widen_shift_mode (enum rtx_code code, rtx op, int count, scalar_int_mode orig_mode, scalar_int_mode mode, enum rtx_code outer_code, HOST_WIDE_INT outer_const)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: A helper to simplify_shift_const_1 to determine the mode we can perform the shift in. The original shift operation CODE is performed on OP in ORIG_MODE. Return the wider mode MODE if we can perform the operation in that mode. Return ORIG_MODE otherwise. We can also assume that the result of the shift is subject to operation OUTER_CODE with operand OUTER_CONST.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_shift_const_1 (enum rtx_code code, machine_mode result_mode, rtx varop, int orig_count)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a shift of VAROP by ORIG_COUNT bits. CODE says what kind of shift. The result of the shift is RESULT_MODE. Return NULL_RTX if we cannot simplify it. Otherwise, return a simplified value. The shift is normally computed in the widest mode we find in VAROP, as long as it isn't a different number of words than RESULT_MODE. Exceptions are ASHIFTRT and ROTATE, which are always done in their original mode.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx simplify_shift_const (rtx x, enum rtx_code code, machine_mode result_mode, rtx varop, int count)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a shift of VAROP by COUNT bits. CODE says what kind of shift. The result of the shift is RESULT_MODE. If we cannot simplify it, return X or, if it is NULL, synthesize the expression with simplify_gen_binary. Otherwise, return a simplified value. The shift is normally computed in the widest mode we find in VAROP, as long as it isn't a different number of words than RESULT_MODE. Exceptions are ASHIFTRT and ROTATE, which are always done in their original mode.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int recog_for_combine_1 (rtx *pnewpat, rtx_insn *insn, rtx *pnotes)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: A subroutine of recog_for_combine. See there for arguments and return value.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool change_zero_ext (rtx pat)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Change every ZERO_EXTRACT and ZERO_EXTEND of a SUBREG that can be expressed as an AND and maybe an LSHIFTRT, to that formulation. Return whether anything was so changed.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int recog_for_combine (rtx *pnewpat, rtx_insn *insn, rtx *pnotes)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Like recog, but we receive the address of a pointer to a new pattern. We try to match the rtx that the pointer points to. If that fails, we may try to modify or replace the pattern, storing the replacement into the same pointer object. Modifications include deletion or addition of CLOBBERs. If the instruction will still not match, we change ZERO_EXTEND and ZERO_EXTRACT to the equivalent AND and perhaps LSHIFTRT patterns, and try with that (and undo if that fails). PNOTES is a pointer to a location where any REG_UNUSED notes added for the CLOBBERs are placed. The value is the final insn code from the pattern ultimately matched, or -1.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx gen_lowpart_for_combine (machine_mode omode, rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Like gen_lowpart_general but for use by combine. In combine it is not possible to create any new pseudoregs. However, it is safe to create invalid memory addresses, because combine will try to recognize them and all they will do is make the combine attempt fail. If for some reason this cannot do its job, an rtx (clobber (const_int 0)) is returned. An insn containing that will not be recognized.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static enum rtx_code simplify_compare_const (enum rtx_code code, machine_mode mode, rtx *pop0, rtx *pop1)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Try to simplify a comparison between OP0 and a constant OP1, where CODE is the comparison code that will be tested, into a (CODE OP0 const0_rtx) form. The result is a possibly different comparison code to use. POP0 and *POP1 may be updated.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static enum rtx_code simplify_comparison (enum rtx_code code, rtx *pop0, rtx *pop1)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Simplify a comparison between *POP0 and *POP1 where CODE is the comparison code that will be tested. The result is a possibly different comparison code to use. *POP0 and POP1 may be updated. It is possible that we might detect that a comparison is either always true or always false. However, we do not perform general constant folding in combine, so this knowledge isn't useful. Such tautologies should have been detected earlier. Hence we ignore all such cases.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static int count_rtxs (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Utility function for record_value_for_reg. Count number of rtxs in X.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void update_table_tick (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Utility function for following routine. Called when X is part of a value being stored into last_set_value. Sets last_set_table_tick for each register mentioned. Similar to mention_regs in cse.cc

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void record_value_for_reg (rtx reg, rtx_insn *insn, rtx value)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Record that REG is set to VALUE in insn INSN. If VALUE is zero, we are saying that the register is clobbered and we no longer know its value. We update reg_stat[], in particular fields last_set, last_set_value, last_set_mode, last_set_nonzero_bits, last_set_sign_bit_copies, last_death, and also the similar information mem_last_set (which insn most recently modified memory) and last_call_luid (which insn was the most recent subroutine call).

gcc/combine.cc.summary: If a SUBREG has the promoted bit set, it is in fact a property of the register present in the SUBREG, so for each such SUBREG go back and adjust nonzero and sign bit information of the registers that are known to have some zero/sign bits set. This is needed because when combine blows the SUBREGs away, the information on zero/sign bits is lost and further combines can be missed because of that.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool reg_truncated_to_mode (machine_mode mode, const_rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Check if X, a register, is known to contain a value already truncated to MODE. In this case we can use a subreg to refer to the truncated value even though in the generic case we would need an explicit truncation.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool record_truncated_value (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: If X is a hard reg or a subreg record the mode that the register is accessed in. For non-TARGET_TRULY_NOOP_TRUNCATION targets we might be able to turn a truncate into a subreg using this information. Return true if traversing X is complete.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void record_truncated_values (rtx *loc, void *data ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Callback for note_uses. Find hardregs and subregs of pseudos and the modes they are used in. This can help truning TRUNCATEs into SUBREGs.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void check_promoted_subreg (rtx_insn *insn, rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Scan X for promoted SUBREGs. For each one found, note what it implies to the registers used in it.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool get_last_value_validate (rtx *loc, rtx_insn *insn, int tick, bool replace)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Verify that all the registers and memory references mentioned in *LOC are still valid. *LOC was part of a value set in INSN when label_tick was equal to TICK. Return false if some are not. If REPLACE is true, replace the invalid references with (clobber (const_int 0)) and return true. This replacement is useful because we often can get useful information about the form of a value (e.g., if it was produced by a shift that always produces -1 or 0) even though we don't know exactly what registers it was produced from.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static rtx get_last_value (const_rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Get the last value assigned to X, if known. Some registers in the value may be replaced with (clobber (const_int 0)) if their value is known longer known reliably.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void reg_dead_at_p_1 (rtx dest, const_rtx x, void *data ATTRIBUTE_UNUSED)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Function called via note_stores from reg_dead_at_p. If DEST is within [reg_dead_regno, reg_dead_endregno), set reg_dead_flag to 1 if X is a CLOBBER and to -1 it is a SET.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool reg_dead_at_p (rtx reg, rtx_insn *insn)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return true if REG is known to be dead at INSN. We scan backwards from INSN. If we hit a REG_DEAD note or a CLOBBER referencing REG, it is dead. If we hit a SET referencing REG, it is live. Otherwise, see if it is live or dead at the start of the basic block we are in. Hard regs marked as being live in NEWPAT_USED_REGS must be assumed to be always live.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void mark_used_regs_combine (rtx x)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Note hard registers in X that are used.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: rtx remove_death (unsigned int regno, rtx_insn *insn)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Remove register number REGNO from the dead registers list of INSN. Return the note used to record the death, if there was one.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void move_deaths (rtx x, rtx maybe_kill_insn, int from_luid, rtx_insn *to_insn, rtx *pnotes)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: For each register (hardware or pseudo) used within expression X, if its death is in an instruction with luid between FROM_LUID (inclusive) and TO_INSN (exclusive), put a REG_DEAD note for that register in the list headed by PNOTES. That said, don't move registers killed by maybe_kill_insn. This is done when X is being merged by combination into TO_INSN. These notes will then be distributed as needed.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool reg_bitfield_target_p (rtx x, rtx body)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Return true if X is the target of a bit-field assignment in BODY, the pattern of an insn. X must be a REG.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void distribute_notes (rtx notes, rtx_insn *from_insn, rtx_insn *i3, rtx_insn *i2, rtx elim_i2, rtx elim_i1, rtx elim_i0)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Given a chain of REG_NOTES originally from FROM_INSN, try to place them as appropriate. I3 and I2 are the insns resulting from the combination insns including FROM (I2 may be zero). ELIM_I2 and ELIM_I1 are either zero or registers that we know will not need REG_DEAD notes because they are being substituted for. This saves searching in the most common cases. Each note in the list is either ignored or placed on some insns, depending on the type of note.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void distribute_links (struct insn_link *links)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Similarly to above, distribute the LOG_LINKS that used to be present on I3, I2, and I1 to new locations. This is also called to add a link pointing at I3 when I3's destination is changed.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static bool unmentioned_reg_p (rtx equiv, rtx expr)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Check for any register or memory mentioned in EQUIV that is not mentioned in EXPR. This is used to restrict EQUIV to "specializations" of EXPR where some registers may have been replaced by constants.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void make_more_copies (void)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Make pseudo-to-pseudo copies after every hard-reg-to-pseudo-copy, because the reg-to-reg copy can usefully combine with later instructions, but we do not want to combine the hard reg into later instructions, for that restricts register allocation.

gcc/combine.cc.signature: static void rest_of_handle_combine (void)
gcc/combine.cc.summary: Try combining insns through substitution.

gcc/reg-stack.cc.signature: static void pop_stack (stack_ptr regstack, int regno)
gcc/reg-stack.cc.summary: Pop a register from the stack.

gcc/reg-stack.cc.summary: Find the hard register number of virtual register REG in REGSTACK. The hard register number is relative to the top of the stack. -1 is returned if the register is not found.

gcc/reg-stack.cc.summary: Emit an insn to pop virtual register REG before or after INSN. REGSTACK is the stack state after INSN and is updated to reflect this pop. WHEN is either emit_insn_before or emit_insn_after. A pop insn is represented as a SET whose destination is the register to be popped and source is the top of stack. A death note for the top of stack cases the movdf pattern to pop.

gcc/reg-stack.cc.signature: static void emit_swap_insn (rtx_insn *insn, stack_ptr regstack, rtx reg)
gcc/reg-stack.cc.summary: Emit an insn before or after INSN to swap virtual register REG with the top of stack. REGSTACK is the stack state before the swap, and is updated to reflect the swap. A swap insn is represented as a PARALLEL of two patterns: each pattern moves one reg to the other. If REG is already at the top of the stack, no insn is emitted.

gcc/reg-stack.cc.signature: static void swap_to_top (rtx_insn *insn, stack_ptr regstack, rtx src1, rtx src2)
gcc/reg-stack.cc.summary: Emit an insns before INSN to swap virtual register SRC1 with the top of stack and virtual register SRC2 with second stack slot. If SRC1 and/or SRC2 are already at the right place, no swap insn is emitted.

gcc/reg-stack.cc.signature: static bool move_for_stack_reg (rtx_insn *insn, stack_ptr regstack, rtx pat)

This function swaps condition in cc users and returns true if successful. It is invoked in 2 different modes, one with DEBUG_SEEN set initially to 0. In this mode, next_flags_user will skip DEBUG_INSNs that it would otherwise return and just sets DEBUG_SEEN to 1 in that case. If DEBUG_SEEN is 0 at the end of toplevel swap_rtx_condition which returns true, it means no problematic DEBUG_INSNs were seen and all changes have been applied. If it returns true but DEBUG_SEEN is 1, it means some problematic DEBUG_INSNs were seen and no changes have been applied so far. In that case one needs to call swap_rtx_condition again with DEBUG_SEEN set to -1, in which case it doesn't skip DEBUG_INSNs, but instead adjusts the flags related condition in them or resets them as needed.

The 387 does have an `fcompp' insn that can pop two regs, but it is sometimes too expensive to do this - a `fcomp' followed by a `fstpl %st(0)' may be easier to set up.

Insns may be emitted as needed to arrange the stack for the 387 based on the contents of the insn. Return whether a control flow insn was deleted in the process.

OLD is the original stack layout, and NEW is the desired form. OLD is updated to reflect the code emitted, i.e., it will be the same as NEW upon return. This function will not preserve block_end[]. reviewed_methods.signature: static machine_mode type_natural_mode (const_tree type, const CUMULATIVE_ARGS *cum, bool in_return)
reviewed_methods.summary: Return the "natural" mode for TYPE. In most cases, this is just TYPE_MODE. But in the case of vector types, it is some vector mode. When we have only some of our vector isa extensions enabled, then there are some modes for which vector_mode_supported_p is false. For these modes, the generic vector support in gcc will choose some non-vector mode in order to implement the type. By computing the natural mode, we'll select the proper ABI location for the operand and not depend on whatever the middle-end decides to do with these vector types. The midde-end can't deal with the vector types > 16 bytes. In this case, we return the original mode and warn ABI change if CUM isn't NULL. If INT_RETURN is true, warn ABI change if the vector mode isn't available for function return value.
reviewed_methods.reason: Unlikely as the primary fix site. This function is about choosing ABI/natural modes for types, especially vectors and calling conventions, not about lowering a local union assignment into a concrete copy sequence.
